BOOK ONE

The keeper climbs the stair

CHAPTER I.

HE keeper climbed the hundred steps{2} every evening at dusk, and every evening the sea answered him with the same grey patience. He trimmed the wick, polished the brass and waited for the ships that rarely came.

The lighthouse at dusk

His daughter kept the logbook in a neat round hand, writing the wind, the weather and the names of the vessels that passed in the night, until the pages filled with ships that had never come home.

CHAPTER II.

MR. ASHDOWN came on a Tuesday with a letter from the Board, and the keeper read it twice by the window before he folded it away without a word to anyone in the house that evening or the next.

The lamp is lit, the tide is low,
 And somewhere out the sailors go.

That night the fog came in thick from the south and the horn sounded until morning, long and low across the water, while the keeper sat beside the great lamp and listened for an answer that did not come.

An Epigraph

"Every light is a promise."

Chapter the Last

In the spring the Board sent a new keeper, a young man with a wireless set and no patience for logbooks, and the old keeper walked down the hundred steps for the last time with his daughter at his side.
